note: HL05 chapter capability ledger. Authored intent, not a derived cache: no validator may rewrite this file. Chapters 1-5 are deliberately absent -- their terminal practice lessons (ML-C01-practice through ML-C05-practice) are still schema v1 with no practises.knowledge, so no payoff can name atoms without inventing them. That absence is real, measurable debt and must not be papered over with placeholders.

chapters.title: Case Endings and Dative Subjects
chapters.label: ch:ml-dative-case
chapters.canDo: I can say that I know Malayalam the way Malayalam itself builds it -- with no subject at all, marking myself with the dative -ikku.

payoff.summary: Say enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām, set it against ñān malayāḷam saṁsārikkunnu, and stack the dative's four Dravidian cousins.

chapters.title: Numbers One to Ten
chapters.label: ch:ml-numbers-one-to-ten
chapters.canDo: I can count from one to ten in Malayalam.

payoff.summary: Count āṟu to pattu, keep the rare ḻ of ēḻu, and take ompatu apart as 'one short of ten'.

chapters.title: Please
chapters.label: ch:ml-please
chapters.canDo: I can say please in Malayalam, and soften a request with the everyday verb ending instead.

payoff.summary: Say dayavāyi, split it into daya 'compassion' plus -vāyi, then use the plainer -u verb ending as the everyday alternative.

chapters.title: Sorry
chapters.label: ch:ml-sorry
chapters.canDo: I can apologise in Malayalam with kṣamikkaṇaṁ, and use the plainer kṣamikkū when it suits.

payoff.summary: Say kṣamikkaṇaṁ, hear the necessitative -aṇaṁ softening it into politeness, then drop to the plain kṣamikkū.

chapters.title: Days of the Week
chapters.label: ch:ml-days-of-the-week
chapters.canDo: I can name the seven days of the Malayalam week and say which planet each one is named for.

payoff.summary: Name the seven planet-days, separate the native ones from the Sanskrit ones, and explain their near-identity with Tamil's.

chapters.title: Four Core Colours
chapters.label: ch:ml-core-colours
chapters.canDo: I can name black, white, red and blue in Malayalam.

payoff.summary: Say karuppŭ, veḷḷa, cuvappŭ and nīla, and mark which three are native Dravidian and which one is a shared Sanskrit loan.

chapters.title: Family
chapters.label: ch:ml-family
chapters.canDo: I can name my father, mother, and my older and younger brothers and sisters in Malayalam.

payoff.summary: Say the six family words in age-graded pairs, and note that Malayalam built its own sibling set rather than tracking Tamil's.

chapters.title: Head and Hand
chapters.label: ch:ml-head-and-hand
chapters.canDo: I can name the head and the hand in Malayalam.

payoff.summary: Say thala and kai, and match them against Tamil's talai and kai.

chapters.title: Seasons
chapters.label: ch:ml-seasons
chapters.canDo: I can name Malayalam's four seasons, including the monsoon that sits at the centre of the year.

payoff.summary: Say vēnalkkālam, mazhakkālam and śaithyakālam as native compounds, then vasanthakālam as the shared Sanskrit loan.

chapters.title: Water and Rice
chapters.label: ch:ml-water-and-rice
chapters.canDo: I can name water and rice in Malayalam, keeping raw ari apart from cooked cōṟu.

payoff.summary: Say veḷḷam and explain why it does not match Tamil's nīr, then split ari from cōṟu.

chapters.title: The Traditional Months
chapters.label: ch:ml-traditional-months
chapters.canDo: I can name the twelve months of the Malayalam Kollam-era calendar and say which zodiac sign each one carries.

payoff.summary: Recite the twelve months from Chiṅṅam, tie Chiṅṅam to Leo, and contrast Malayalam's zodiac naming with Tamil's nakshatras.

chapters.title: Noon and Midnight
chapters.label: ch:ml-noon-and-midnight
chapters.canDo: I can say noon and midnight in Malayalam and hear paathi, 'half', inside paathira.

payoff.summary: Say pāthira, pull pāthi out of it, and show it is a native half-word rather than Sanskrit ardha.

chapters.title: Telling Time
chapters.label: ch:ml-telling-time
chapters.canDo: I can say the hour in Malayalam with maṇi, as in oru maṇi, one o'clock.

payoff.summary: Say maṇi for hour, bell and gem, then oru maṇi, and state where Malayalam's and Tamil's dictionaries disagree about it.

chapters.title: Asking Someone's Age
chapters.label: ch:ml-asking-age
chapters.canDo: I can ask how old someone is in Malayalam and answer with a dative subject.

payoff.summary: Ask ningaḷkku ethra vayassuṇṭŭ? and answer enikku irupatu vayassuṇṭŭ -- 'to me twenty age exists'.

chapters.title: Numbers 11–20 and Weather
chapters.label: ch:ml-numbers-and-weather
chapters.canDo: I can count from eleven to twenty in Malayalam and say what the weather is doing.

payoff.summary: Say kālāvastha as 'the state of time', split it into kālam and avastha, and add mazha peyyunnu for rain.

chapters.title: Dog and Cat
chapters.label: ch:ml-dog-and-cat
chapters.canDo: I can name a dog and a cat in Malayalam.

payoff.summary: Say nāya on the shared Dravidian dog-root, then pūcha, which follows Tamil's cat-word rather than Kannada's.

chapters.title: Green and Yellow
chapters.label: ch:ml-green-and-yellow
chapters.canDo: I can name green and yellow in Malayalam and say why the two come from unrelated roots.

payoff.summary: Say paccha beside Tamil paccai and mañña beside mañcaḷ, and show they are not doublets of each other.

chapters.title: Day
chapters.label: ch:ml-day
chapters.canDo: I can use divasam for an everyday day in Malayalam and still recognise native nāḷ where it survives.

payoff.summary: Find nāḷ alive inside nāḷe, oru nāḷ and piṟannāḷ, and answer whether Sanskrit divasam erased it.

chapters.title: Night
chapters.label: ch:ml-night
chapters.canDo: I can say night in Malayalam with rāthri and tell literary iravŭ apart from everyday iruḷ, 'darkness'.

payoff.summary: Sort iravŭ from iruḷ by the job each one still does in the modern language.

chapters.title: Good Night
chapters.label: ch:ml-good-night
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone good night in Malayalam with śubha rāthri.

payoff.summary: Say śubha rāthri as 'auspicious night', and mark the English code-switching claim as thinly sourced and not unique to Malayalam.

chapters.title: Morning
chapters.label: ch:ml-morning
chapters.canDo: I can say morning in Malayalam with rāvile and hear the night-word hidden inside it.

payoff.summary: Say rāvile, pull rāvŭ 'night' out of it, and place prabhātaṁ beside it as the Sanskrit alternative.

chapters.title: Evening
chapters.label: ch:ml-evening
chapters.canDo: I can say evening in Malayalam with vaikunnēraṁ, 'latening time'.

payoff.summary: Say vaikunnēraṁ, trace it to vaikuka 'to get late', and flag that sources disagree on whether it also covers afternoon.

chapters.title: Afternoon
chapters.label: ch:ml-afternoon
chapters.canDo: I can say afternoon in Malayalam as uchakaḻiññ -- literally 'noon having passed'.

payoff.summary: Build uchakaḻiññ from ucha plus kaḻiyuka, and contrast it with Telugu, which widened its noon-word instead.

chapters.title: Good Morning
chapters.label: ch:ml-good-morning
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone in the morning in Malayalam with suprabhātaṁ.

payoff.summary: Say suprabhātaṁ, split su- from prabhātaṁ, and show it is NOT built on śubha the way good night is.

chapters.title: Good Evening
chapters.label: ch:ml-good-evening
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone in the evening in Malayalam with śubha sāyāhnaṁ.

payoff.summary: Say śubha sāyāhnaṁ, note it is built on the poetic sāyāhnaṁ rather than native vaikunnēraṁ, and follow sāya back to PIE.

chapters.title: Good Afternoon
chapters.label: ch:ml-good-afternoon
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone in the afternoon in Malayalam with śubha madhyāhnaṁ, and say how it differs from the everyday afternoon word.

payoff.summary: Line up the three sister languages' everyday afternoon words and show where all three converge on śubha + madhyāhna.

chapters.title: The Core Verbs
chapters.label: ch:ml-core-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can build a Malayalam verb as stem plus one ending with no person marking at all, swap that ending for past, future or mood, and say why 'I know Malayalam' puts me in the dative instead of the subject slot.

payoff.summary: Say എനിക്ക് മലയാളം അറിയാം, name the two slots that built irikkunnu, pōkunnu and kāṇunnu, and explain why this verb moves the knower out of the subject slot altogether.
